concepts.title: Food Science, Processing, Technology and Manufacturing
concepts.definition: Food science studies the make-up and behaviour of foods from harvest to plate; food processing converts raw ingredients into finished or semi finished goods; food technology applies that science, with economic and legal rules, to produce foods at scale, and food manufacturing is the mass production that results.
concepts.formula: chain -- raw material to processing to technology to manufacturing
concepts.key_idea: Technology must also keep processing safe, sustainable and free of waste.
question_patterns: explain the terms food science, food processing, food technology and food manufacturing
how does food science differ from food technology
what does food processing do to raw ingredients
why is food manufacturing called a large scale activity
how does food technology promote sustainability

solution_steps.action: define each term in its own line
solution_steps.explain: science studies, processing transforms, technology applies, manufacturing scales up

solution_steps.action: connect them in sequence
solution_steps.explain: each stage feeds the next, ending in marketable safe foods

worked_examples.q: Which discipline studies the make-up and behaviour of foods: food science or astronomy?

concepts.title: Historic Milestones of Food Technology
concepts.section: Development of Food Processing and Technology
concepts.definition: Modern food technology began with Appert's canning breakthrough in 1810 and gained a scientific base when Pasteur explained spoilage of wine in 1864 and devised milk pasteurisation; wars and space travel later pushed convenience foods forward.
concepts.formula: timeline -- 1810 canning, 1864 pasteurisation, twentieth century convenience foods
concepts.key_idea: Military needs, space exploration and working women's demands shaped the convenience foods of today.
question_patterns: trace the development of food technology from canning to convenience foods
who developed the canning process and in which year
what did Louis Pasteur contribute to food science
what is pasteurisation and why was it a major advance
how did wars and space exploration push food technology forward
which products were developed specially for working women

solution_steps.action: place the milestones on the timeline
solution_steps.explain: canning 1810, pasteurisation 1864, then twentieth century growth

solution_steps.action: link each milestone to its driver
solution_steps.explain: preservation for armies, safety science for milk, convenience for new lifestyles

worked_examples.q: Who devised milk pasteurisation: Pasteur or Appert?

concepts.title: Food Spoilage and Its Causes
concepts.section: Importance of Food Processing and Preservation
concepts.definition: Foods decay through physical, chemical and biological attack -- pests, insects, wrong storage temperatures, light, oxygen, moisture, microbes and the food's own enzymes -- losing flavour, texture, colour and nourishment until they turn unsafe.
concepts.formula: spoilage = microbes plus enzymes plus environment acting on food
concepts.key_idea: Enzymes are protein catalysts inside the food itself, so decay starts even without outside germs.
question_patterns: what causes food spoilage and makes food unfit to eat
list the factors that lead to deterioration of stored food
how do naturally present enzymes spoil fresh produce
which micro organisms are the main agents of spoilage
how do light, oxygen and moisture damage food quality

solution_steps.action: group the causes: biological, chemical, physical
solution_steps.explain: bacteria, fungi, yeasts and moulds; enzymatic browning; light and moisture damage

solution_steps.action: describe the visible outcomes
solution_steps.explain: off flavours, weak texture, discolouration, nutrient loss, unsafe product

worked_examples.q: Protein catalysts inside the food itself that drive decay are called what?

concepts.title: Perishability Classes of Foods
concepts.section: Classes of Foods Based on Perishability
concepts.definition: Foods sort into three keeping classes: perishables such as milk, curd, fish and meat that fail within a day or two; semi perishables like fruits and vegetables that hold for a fortnight, with root crops lasting two to four weeks; and non perishables such as grains, pulses and oilseeds that keep about a year.
concepts.formula: class ladder -- days for perishables, weeks for semi perishables, a year for non perishables
concepts.key_idea: Root crops sit at the top of the semi perishable band; dry grains anchor the year long end.
question_patterns: classify foods on the basis of perishability with examples
how long can semi perishable foods be stored
which foods count as non perishable and why do they keep so long
name two perishable foods and state their safe keeping time
where do potatoes and onions fall on the perishability scale

solution_steps.action: define the three classes with their time bands
solution_steps.explain: one or two days, up to two weeks or four for roots, and about a year

solution_steps.action: attach examples to each band
solution_steps.explain: milk and fish; fruits, vegetables, onions, potatoes; rice, wheat, pulses, oilseeds

worked_examples.q: Milk, curd, fish and meat fall in which keeping class: perishable or non-perishable?

concepts.title: Principles of Preservation
concepts.section: Basic concepts in food processing methods
concepts.definition: Processing holds spoilage back by five levers: applying heat, withdrawing water, chilling during storage, cutting acidity, and limiting contact with oxygen -- each one starves microbes or enzymes of what they need to work.
concepts.formula: five levers -- heat, water removal, low temperature, reduced pH, controlled oxygen
concepts.key_idea: Microbial growth depends on nutrients, moisture, pH, oxygen and inhibitors, so each lever targets one growth factor.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe104.txt, basic concepts to prevent spoilage (approx lines 201-228)
question_patterns: what is done in food processing to extend shelf life
list the five principles used to prevent food spoilage
how does removal of moisture preserve a food
why does lowering the pH keep food safe
which preservation lever targets oxygen dependent spoilage
what four conditions do bacteria need to grow and multiply

solution_steps.action: state the five levers
solution_steps.explain: heat treatment, drying, refrigeration, acidification, oxygen exclusion

solution_steps.action: match each lever to the growth factor it blocks
solution_steps.explain: moisture, warmth, acidity and air each let microbes multiply when unchecked

worked_examples.q: Which preservation lever withdraws moisture: drying or chilling?

concepts.title: Classes of Processed Foods
concepts.definition: Processed products range from minimally processed fresh cuts, through preserved frozen, dehydrated and canned goods, to manufactured items like pickles and jams, formulated bakes and frozen desserts, purified food derivatives such as sugar and vanaspati, plus functional and medical foods.
concepts.formula: class ladder -- minimal to preserved to manufactured to formulated to derivatives to functional to medical
concepts.key_idea: The deeper the processing, the further the product sits from the raw character of its ingredients.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe104.txt, classification of processed foods (approx lines 247-275)
question_patterns: classify processed foods on the basis of extent and type of processing
differentiate between preserved foods and manufactured foods
what are formulated foods and give two examples
how is vanaspati obtained from oil and what is the process called
what makes a food functional and give one example
which class suits a person with lactose intolerance

solution_steps.action: walk up the seven classes in order
solution_steps.explain: cleaned cut produce, frozen dehydrated canned goods, pickle jam products, bread biscuit mixes, sugar and hydrogenated oils, probiotics, medical foods

solution_steps.action: note the character change at each step
solution_steps.explain: minimal processing keeps freshness; formulated and derivative products lose the original identity

worked_examples.q: Sugar and vanaspati are which class of processed food: derivatives or minimal?

concepts.title: Fortification and Nutrient Modification
concepts.definition: Staple diets built on cereals miss certain nutrients, so producers add the missing nutrient to common foods -- iodine in salt, folic acid in flour, vitamins A and D in milk and oils -- or re-engineer recipes with sweeteners and fat substitutes to cut calories.
concepts.formula: fortified food = staple plus added nutrient
concepts.key_idea: FSSAI sets the standards so fortified staples deliver minimum dietary needs; treated proteins can mimic fat texture with less energy.
question_patterns: what is food fortification and why is it needed
name two staples that are fortified and the nutrients added to them
which body sets standards for fortification of staple foods in India
how do food scientists cut the calorie content of processed foods
how is fat replaced in ice cream while keeping the smooth texture
why are cereal based diets prone to deficiency disorders

solution_steps.action: define fortification with staple examples
solution_steps.explain: iodised salt, fortified flour, vitamin enriched milk and oils

solution_steps.action: extend to engineered foods
solution_steps.explain: artificial sweeteners and protein based fat replacers lower energy while holding taste and texture

worked_examples.q: Which nutrient is added to salt: iodine or iron?

concepts.title: Careers, Skills and Self Employment in Food Technology
concepts.section: Preparing for a career and Scope
concepts.definition: The industry needs technologists who know food chemistry, microbiology, quality assurance and packaging, can run sensory tests and design briefs, and may grow from production and quality roles into research, consultancy or their own small scale venture with bank and government support.
concepts.formula: career ladder -- diploma or degree to industry roles to research or entrepreneurship
concepts.key_idea: Self employment can start tiny -- pickles, salted peanuts, water pouches -- with finance, training and marketing support from banks and the state.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe104.txt, career, scope and self employment sections (approx lines 400-551)
question_patterns: what knowledge and skills does the food industry expect from a technologist
list the career avenues open in food processing and technology

name the institutes offering specialised food technology education in India
what support can an entrepreneur expect while starting a food processing unit
give two examples of low investment self employment ventures in food processing
in which departments of the food industry do technologists work

solution_steps.action: map the qualification route
solution_steps.explain: certificates and diplomas for small units, degrees and research qualifications for industry and academia, CFTRI and NIFTEM for specialisation

solution_steps.action: list the roles and the self employment option
solution_steps.explain: production, quality, R&D, marketing, teaching; entrepreneurs get finance, training, infrastructure and marketing help

worked_examples.q: Self-employment can start tiny with pickles, salted peanuts or which sealed drink packs: water pouches or oil drums?

concepts.title: Industry Share Arithmetic
concepts.definition: The food industry's contribution to any national total -- GDP, exports or industrial investment -- is that stated percentage of the total, so the rupee or dollar value follows by applying the share to the base figure.
concepts.key_idea: The sector is ranked fifth in size, adds about six percent of GDP and thirteen percent of exports.
question_patterns: the food industry contributes 6 percent of a GDP of 20000000 crore rupees; compute its contribution in crore rupees
if the sector accounts for 13 percent of exports worth 2500000 crore rupees, calculate the export earnings from processed food
find the rupee value of an industry contribution when the share percentage and the national total are given
a segment involves 6 percent of total industrial investment of 500000 crore rupees; how much does it involve
compute the GDP contribution of a sector whose share and the GDP figure are stated

solution_steps.action: apply the share percentage to the base
solution_steps.explain: multiply the base by the percentage and divide by one hundred

worked_examples.q: The food industry adds about what percent of GDP: six or sixty?

concepts.title: Danger Zone Temperature Span
concepts.definition: Bacteria multiply at any temperature inside the danger zone, so the width of that zone in degrees is simply the upper limit minus the lower limit -- the range a kitchen must keep food out of.
concepts.key_idea: The zone runs from 5 to 60 degrees Celsius, a 55 degree window in which bacteria thrive.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe104.txt, Did You Know box (approx lines 229-241)
question_patterns: bacteria grow between 5 and 60 degrees Celsius; what is the span of the danger zone in degrees
find the width of the temperature band in which bacteria multiply when the two limits are stated
a kitchen monitor logs 40 degrees Celsius; how many degrees does it sit above the lower danger zone limit
calculate how wide the danger zone is if the ceiling is 60 and the floor is 5 degrees
by how many degrees does the upper danger limit exceed the lower one

solution_steps.action: subtract the lower limit from the upper limit
solution_steps.explain: the difference gives the width of the risky band

worked_examples.q: The danger zone runs from 5 to how many degrees Celsius: 60 or 6?

concepts.title: Shelf Life in Days
concepts.section: Classes of Foods Based on Perishability
concepts.definition: Storage classes quote keeping times in days, weeks or years; a week long band converts to days by multiplying by seven, letting you compare all classes on one scale.
concepts.key_idea: Semi perishables keep one to two weeks, that is 7 to 14 days, while non perishables stretch to a full year.
question_patterns: a semi perishable lot keeps for 2 weeks; express its shelf life in days
convert a stated keeping time in weeks into days for a storage plan
if fruits last 1 week and root crops last 3 weeks, how many days does each class keep
a consignment of onions is stored for 4 weeks; how many days of shelf life is that
how many days of storage does a 2 week vegetable allowance amount to

solution_steps.action: multiply the weeks by seven
solution_steps.explain: seven days make one week, so the product is the day count

worked_examples.q: Semi-perishables keep one to two weeks, that is at most how many days: 14 or 140?

concepts.title: Costing a Preserved Product
concepts.section: Practical 1: design, prepare and evaluate a processed product
concepts.definition: The full cost of a homemade preserved product adds the raw materials, energy used, labour and packing material, and dividing by the number of units gives the cost of one jar or pouch -- the number a label must justify.
concepts.key_idea: Every input counts: a 500 gram batch must price its fuel and its jar, not only its fruit.
question_patterns: a pickle batch uses Rs 60 of raw material, Rs 10 of energy, Rs 30 of labour and Rs 20 of packing for 4 jars; find the cost per jar
calculate the cost of one unit when the four cost heads of a preserved product and the number of units are given
find the per unit cost of a murabba batch whose materials, energy, labour and packing costs are stated for the whole batch
a group makes 5 bottles of squash at a total batch cost of Rs 150; what does one bottle cost to make
work out the unit cost from the batch total and the count of packaged units

solution_steps.action: sum the four cost heads
solution_steps.explain: materials plus energy plus labour plus packing is the whole batch cost

solution_steps.action: divide by the units made
solution_steps.explain: the quotient is the cost of a single jar, bottle or pouch

worked_examples.q: Full cost of a homemade preserve adds material, energy, labour and what else: packing or gossip?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A group prepares 4 jars of pickle with {material_cost} rupees of ingredients, {energy_cost} rupees of fuel, {labour_cost} rupees of labour and {packing_cost} rupees of jars. Find the cost of one jar.
